idiom_name: named flag registry read from configuration at a single toggle point
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: keep a registry of named flags whose values are loaded from configuration (versioned file, environment, database or key-value store) at start-up and refreshed in the background where a restart is not acceptable; the toggle point asks the registry once and dispatches to one of two implementations. Encapsulate the decision - a boolean, a predicate or a decision object - and inject it into the code that branches, so business code depends on the decision and not on the flag infrastructure; if the same check appears twice, replace it with polymorphic substitution. Give every flag an owner, a lifetime and a safe default: release and experiment flags are temporary and must be deleted after rollout, ops and permission flags are long-lived and need defaults, audit and an off state that is safe rather than merely convenient.
code_sketch:
flags = FlagRegistry.load(source)            # one source of truth, defaults included
if flags.enabled("new-checkout", context):   # toggle point - ideally one per feature
    new_checkout(context)
else:
    legacy_checkout(context)
pitfalls: Repeating the same flag check in many places makes the live behaviour unreconstructable; funnel it through one decision point or a strategy selection.
Treating a flag as an ordinary long-lived configuration value: without an owner and a removal date it leaves a dead branch behind for years.
Letting the flag registry become a hidden dependency of business code, so tests and library reuse must drag the whole toggling infrastructure along.

Wrong move: reusing the name of a completed flag for new work -> the obsolete code path the old flag guarded wakes up again under the new one, the mechanism behind Knight Capital's $460M loss -> mint a fresh key per feature and delete the old flag together with its dead branch.

Wrong move: a single global "all flags on" developer override -> one bad config push exposes every unreleased feature at once, as in LinkedIn's "flags all on" incident -> scope overrides per flag and per environment and make the off state the default.

Wrong move: relying on a comment or reminder to delete a flag later -> most flags are never removed and quietly harden into permanent debt -> enforce expiry dates in the flag registry and automate stale-flag detection in CI.
